tools.name: Free SEO audit
tools.job: Audit a whole site and get a ranked list of real problems.
tools.metaDescription: Run a free SEO audit on any website. Real findings in about 30 seconds, no account and no card. Up to 25 pages crawled.
checks: Missing, duplicate or over-long title tags
Meta description length and duplication
More than one H1, or no H1 at all
Missing or conflicting canonical tags
A noindex left in production
robots.txt rules that conflict with your meta robots
Missing Open Graph and Twitter card tags
Thin pages by word count
Broken internal links
Oversized images and missing alt text
No structured data at all
Slow time to first byte
Mixed content on an HTTPS page
A page that no sitemap references

tools.name: SEO checker
tools.metaDescription: Check a single page for on-page SEO problems: title, meta, headings, word count, links, images and schema. Free, no signup.
checks: Everything the site audit checks, for a single URL
Word count and content-to-code ratio
The full heading outline, in document order
Keyword distribution, counted not guessed
Internal and external link counts
Image count, bytes and alt coverage

tools.name: Website SEO score
tools.job: Turn the audit into one score you can share.
tools.metaDescription: Get a 0–100 SEO score for any website, with sub-scores for content, technical, performance and metadata. Free and shareable.
checks: A 0–100 overall score, built from the audit findings
Four sub-scores: content, technical, performance and metadata
The weighting used, published so the number is not a black box
A shareable card that expires in 30 days and can be removed at any time

tools.name: Meta tag checker
tools.job: Inspect metadata and see how it truncates.
tools.metaDescription: Inspect the title, meta description, canonical, robots, Open Graph and Twitter tags on any page, with pixel-width truncation warnings.
checks: Title and description length in characters and in pixels
Where each one truncates in a search result
Canonical tag presence and whether it is self-referencing
Meta robots and X-Robots-Tag, including conflicts
Open Graph tags needed for a link preview
Twitter card tags

tools.name: Sitemap checker
tools.job: Validate an XML sitemap and sample its URLs.
tools.metaDescription: Validate an XML sitemap: structure, size limits, nesting, lastmod dates, and whether the URLs in it actually return 200.
checks: Valid XML and the right namespace
More than 50,000 URLs or over 50 MB uncompressed
Sitemap index nesting handled correctly
A sample of up to 50 URLs fetched for their real status
URLs listed in the sitemap but blocked by robots.txt
Missing or implausible lastmod values

tools.name: Robots.txt tester
tools.job: Test a path against robots.txt and see which rule wins.
tools.metaDescription: Test any path against a live robots.txt and see exactly which rule matches, for which user-agent, and why.
checks: Which rule matches your path, and why that one wins
Longest-match precedence, the rule most people get wrong
Whether you have accidentally blocked the whole site
Whether a sitemap directive is present
Per user-agent differences, including Googlebot and Bingbot

tools.name: Broken link checker
tools.job: Find broken links on a page.
tools.metaDescription: Find broken links on any page. Checks up to 200 links for 4xx, 5xx, timeouts, redirect chains and mixed content.
checks: Up to 200 links from one page
4xx and 5xx responses
Timeouts and connection failures
Redirect chains worth shortening
Links to http:// from an https:// page

tools.name: Redirect checker
tools.job: Follow a redirect chain, hop by hop.
tools.metaDescription: Follow a URL through every redirect hop. See the status at each step, spot loops, and find 302s that should be 301s.
checks: Every hop, in order, with its status code
Chain length, and whether it is worth collapsing
Redirect loops
A 302 where a 301 almost certainly belongs
A hop that drops from https to http
The final status and address

tools.name: Schema markup validator
tools.metaDescription: Validate structured data on a page or paste your own JSON-LD. Checks types, required properties and conflicting blocks.
checks: Whether the JSON-LD parses at all
Recognised and unrecognised @type values
Required properties missing for the declared type
Recommended properties worth adding
Two blocks that contradict each other
Markup describing something that is not on the page

tools.name: Page speed checker
tools.job: Measure what the document itself costs.
tools.metaDescription: Measure time to first byte, document size, render-blocking resources and image payload. A lab measurement, and we say so.
checks: Time to first byte, measured from our server
HTML document size before images and scripts
Render-blocking stylesheets and scripts in the head
Total image payload declared on the page
Compression and caching headers

tools.name: Hreflang checker
tools.metaDescription: Check hreflang annotations on any page. We fetch each alternate and verify the return tag, which is where most setups break.
checks: Every hreflang annotation on the page
Whether each alternate links back — the return tag
Invalid language or region codes
A missing self-reference
A missing or duplicated x-default
Alternates that redirect or 404

tools.name: Image SEO checker
tools.job: Check every image on a page.
tools.metaDescription: Check every image on a page for missing alt text, oversized files, missing dimensions and the wrong format for the job.
checks: Images with no alt attribute
Decorative images given alt text they should not have
Files larger than they need to be
A JPEG or PNG where AVIF or WebP belongs
Missing width and height, which causes layout shift
No loading hint on images below the fold

tools.name: SERP preview
tools.job: Preview a search result before you publish it.
tools.metaDescription: Preview how your title and description appear in search results, measured in pixels rather than characters.
checks: Desktop and mobile widths, measured in pixels
Where the title truncates
Where the description truncates
How the URL is displayed as a breadcrumb

tools.name: Keyword questions
tools.job: Turn one term into the questions around it.
tools.metaDescription: Expand a seed term into the questions people ask around it. Deterministic patterns, grouped by question type.
checks: Question expansion across who, what, when, where, why, how and which
Comparison and alternative patterns
Cost, time and difficulty patterns
Grouped output you can take straight into a content brief
No AI, so the same seed always gives the same list

tools.name: SEO checklist
tools.job: Work through SEO task by task.
tools.metaDescription: Work through a practical SEO checklist, grouped by job. Your progress is kept in your own browser.
checks: Grouped by job: technical, on-page, content, local and beyond Google
Progress kept in your own browser, not on our server
Each item links to the tool that checks it
Nothing to sign up for

platform.name: Site audit and SEO Center
platform.summary: Audit, fix, review and publish SEO changes, with a history you can roll back.
platform.problem: You already know your site has SEO problems. You have probably run a crawler and got a spreadsheet of 400 rows. The spreadsheet is not the problem — the problem is that nothing in it ever gets fixed, because fixing means a ticket, a developer, a deploy, and six weeks.

steps.title: The audit runs on a schedule
steps.body: A sweep reads your pages, sitemap, robots.txt and redirects. Free sites run weekly; paid sites daily or hourly. You do not have to remember to check.

steps.title: Findings become an issue list, not a report
steps.body: Each finding is a tracked item with a severity, an owner and a state. It stays open until it is fixed or deliberately dismissed, and dismissing it is a recorded decision.

steps.title: The SEO Center drafts the change
steps.body: For the fixable classes of issue — titles, descriptions, canonicals, redirects, schema — it writes the actual replacement rather than telling you to.

steps.title: A human approves a release
steps.body: Changes are grouped into a release. Someone reviews the diff and approves it or sends it back. Nothing goes live on its own.

steps.title: It publishes, and you can undo it
steps.body: On supported platforms the release publishes directly. The history records what changed, who approved it and when, and the rollback is one click.

limits.free: Unlimited on-demand audits on one website, crawling up to 500 URLs per run, with the whole SEO Center included.
limits.paid: Growth raises the crawl to 10,000 URLs and the cadence to daily; Business goes to 100,000 URLs and hourly.
limits.cannot: It does not render JavaScript during the public crawl, it cannot see anything behind a login, and direct publishing depends on your platform — see the publishing page for exactly where.

faqs.question: How is this different from running Screaming Frog?
faqs.answer: Screaming Frog crawls better than we do on very large sites. It then stops. We continue: the finding becomes a tracked issue, a drafted change, an approval and a published page.

faqs.question: Will it change my site without asking?
faqs.answer: No. Every change goes into a release that a person has to approve. There is no mode where it publishes unreviewed SEO changes.

platform.name: Page SEO and on-page
platform.summary: Per-page titles, meta, social cards, schema, the page checklist and URL triage.
platform.problem: Titles and meta descriptions are the highest-leverage thing on a page and the most likely to be wrong. They get written once, by whoever built the page, and then never looked at again — so you end up with forty pages sharing one description and a homepage title that says "Home".

steps.title: Every page gets a record
steps.body: Title, description, canonical, robots directives, social cards and schema for each URL, in one list you can sort by what is missing.

steps.title: The page checklist shows what is incomplete
steps.body: Per page, not per site: which of the on-page essentials are present, which are missing, and which are present but wrong.

steps.title: Edit the metadata where you can see it
steps.body: Change the title and description with the search-result preview beside them, so you see the truncation before you publish it rather than after.

steps.title: URL triage catches the duplicates
steps.body: Pages competing for the same intent are grouped so you can merge, redirect or differentiate them — the mistake that quietly costs the most.

limits.free: The whole of Page SEO on one website, with no page-count limit beyond the crawl cap.
limits.paid: Higher crawl ceilings, so a large catalogue is covered in one run.
limits.cannot: It can only edit metadata it can publish. On an unsupported platform it produces the exact change and an export instead.

faqs.question: Does it rewrite my titles automatically?
faqs.answer: It drafts them. Publishing requires an approved release, and on the free plan AI-written suggestions come out of your 50-post allowance only when you use the AI writer.

platform.name: Technical SEO
platform.summary: Health checks, sitemap, robots, redirects, a 404 monitor, crawl intelligence and site quality.
platform.problem: Technical SEO fails quietly. A sitemap that stopped updating, a redirect chain four hops long, a noindex that shipped with a staging config — none of it throws an error, and you usually find out when traffic has already gone.

steps.title: Health checks run server-side on a schedule
steps.body: Pages are fetched from our servers, not from your browser, so the check is the same whoever is logged in.

steps.title: Sitemap and robots.txt are managed, not just read
steps.body: See what is in the sitemap, what should be, and what robots.txt is blocking that you did not mean to block.

steps.title: Redirects are a map you can edit
steps.body: Chains, loops and 302s that should be 301s are listed, and the redirect map is editable and versioned.

steps.title: The 404 monitor watches what actually breaks
steps.body: Real missing URLs with the pages linking to them, so you fix the ones that cost you something.

steps.title: Crawl intelligence shows the shape of the site
steps.body: Click depth, orphan pages, and the sections consuming crawl budget without earning it.

limits.free: Health checks, sitemap, robots, redirects and the 404 monitor on one website, weekly, up to 500 URLs per crawl.
limits.paid: Daily or hourly checks, and crawls large enough for a real catalogue.
limits.cannot: It does not execute JavaScript on the public crawl, it cannot read server logs, and editing robots.txt or redirects live requires a supported publish path.

faqs.question: Can it edit my robots.txt?
faqs.answer: Where there is a supported publish path, yes, through an approved release with a rollback. Elsewhere it gives you the exact file to put in place.

faqs.question: Does it handle redirect chains?
faqs.answer: It finds them, shows every hop, and proposes the single redirect that replaces the chain.

platform.name: Keyword intelligence
platform.summary: Rankings, a keyword library, research imports, and the Question Bank for AI-era queries.
platform.problem: Rank tracking tells you a number went down. It rarely tells you which page lost it, what else moved at the same time, or what people are actually asking now that answers come from an AI rather than ten blue links.

steps.title: Track the keywords that matter
steps.body: Positions over time, with the URL that ranks, so a drop points at a page instead of a mystery.

steps.title: Build a keyword library
steps.body: One place for the terms you care about, grouped by topic, shared across content planning and the audit.

steps.title: Import the research you already have
steps.body: Bring CSV exports from wherever you did your research. We do not pretend our dataset is the biggest, so we make it easy to use somebody else’s.

steps.title: The Question Bank collects AI-era queries
steps.body: The questions people ask in full sentences — the shape that matters when an assistant is answering rather than a results page.

limits.free: 200 tracked keywords on one website, the full keyword library, research imports and the Question Bank.
limits.cannot: Our keyword database is smaller than Semrush’s or Ahrefs’. We say so on the comparison pages. If dataset size is your bottleneck, buy one of theirs and import into this.

faqs.question: How big is your keyword database?
faqs.answer: Smaller than the market leaders, and we are not going to claim otherwise. Tracking, the library and the Question Bank are strong; raw research volume is not where we compete.

faqs.question: How often do rankings update?
faqs.answer: Weekly on the free plan, daily on Growth and hourly on Business.

platform.name: Links and authority
platform.summary: Internal linking suggestions, backlinks and authority tracking.
platform.problem: Internal linking is the cheapest ranking improvement available and almost nobody does it, because doing it properly means holding your whole site in your head at once.

steps.title: Suggestions come from your own content
steps.body: Pages that should link to each other, based on what they are actually about, with the anchor text proposed.

steps.title: Apply a suggestion as a tracked change
steps.body: Accepted links go into a release like any other change, so they are reviewed and reversible.

steps.title: Backlinks and authority are tracked alongside
steps.body: Referring domains and authority over time, so an internal change and an external one can be read together.

limits.free: Internal linking suggestions in full. Backlinks and authority are read-only.
limits.paid: Growth and Business unlock the full backlink workspace.
limits.cannot: Our backlink index is far smaller than Ahrefs’. For serious link research, theirs is the better tool and we will not pretend otherwise.

faqs.question: Is your backlink index competitive?
faqs.answer: No. Ahrefs and Semrush have far larger indexes built over far longer. Internal linking is where we are genuinely strong, because it only needs your own site.

platform.name: Beyond Google
platform.summary: Bing, Yandex, Naver, Seznam, Baidu, Brave; IndexNow; Image Search; AI and agent traffic.
platform.problem: Nearly every SEO tool is a Google tool with other engines bolted on, if at all. If a meaningful share of your traffic comes from Bing, from Yandex, from Naver, or increasingly from an AI assistant quoting you, you are flying blind on most of your search surface.

steps.title: Connect the engines you care about
steps.body: Bing Webmaster Tools and Search Console connect through your own grant. Others are covered through our own crawling and submission.

steps.title: Submit through IndexNow
steps.body: New and changed URLs are pushed to the participating engines — Bing, Yandex and Seznam — instead of waiting to be discovered.

steps.title: See your image-search inventory
steps.body: Which images are indexable, which are missing alt text, and which are too heavy to be served well.

steps.title: Report AI and agent traffic
steps.body: Requests arriving from AI assistants and agents, separated from ordinary referrals, so "nobody clicks any more" becomes a number instead of a worry.

limits.free: All six non-Google engines, Image Search inventory, IndexNow submission and AI-traffic reporting, on one website.
limits.paid: Higher cadence and volume, not a different feature set. This is deliberately not a paid wedge.
limits.cannot: The engines do not expose the same data. Bing and Google give rich webmaster data; others give very little, and we show what each one actually provides rather than inventing parity.

faqs.question: Do you get the same data from every engine?
faqs.answer: No, and anyone claiming to does not. Google and Bing provide detailed webmaster data. For the others we rely on our own crawling and on IndexNow, and each engine block says exactly what it covers.

faqs.question: What counts as AI traffic?
faqs.answer: Requests whose user-agent or referrer identifies an AI assistant or agent. It is a measurement of what reaches your server, not an estimate of what an assistant said about you.

platform.name: Local SEO and reputation
platform.summary: A location registry, landing-page checks, and the review platforms you are missing.
platform.problem: Local SEO fails on the boring things: an address written three different ways, a landing page that never mentions the city, and four review platforms your competitors are on and you are not.

steps.title: Register your locations
steps.body: Each location with its address, hours and service area, in one place rather than scattered across pages.

steps.title: Check the landing pages
steps.body: Whether each location page actually carries the signals a local result needs, and which ones are duplicates of each other with the city swapped.

steps.title: Work the review-platform checklist
steps.body: The platforms relevant to your sector, which you are present on, and which you are not.

limits.free: One location, with landing-page checks and the full review-platform checklist.
limits.paid: Growth covers 25 locations; Business is unlimited.
limits.cannot: It does not post to review platforms for you and does not manage replies. It tells you where you should be and what is wrong with the pages you have.

faqs.question: Does it manage my Google Business Profile?
faqs.answer: It checks the signals your location pages send and tracks the platforms you should be listed on. Posting and replying stay with you.

platform.name: Content engine
platform.summary: Strategy and calendar, content clusters, Blog Studio, Auto Blog, help centre and newsletter.
platform.problem: You have been told to publish more. You have also seen what "publish more" does to a site when it means AI-written filler, and you would rather have no blog than that one.

steps.title: Plan around clusters, not one-off posts
steps.body: Topics grouped into clusters with a hub page and supporting pages, so the content has a shape instead of being a list.

steps.title: Draft in Blog Studio
steps.body: A draft is generated from a brief, a title or a keyword — and then it waits. Blog Studio holds an approve-to-publish lock.

steps.title: A human approves before anything goes live
steps.body: This is a lock, not a setting we encourage you to turn off. Nothing publishes to your site without a person agreeing to it.

steps.title: A brand check runs on every post
steps.body: Posts are checked against your brand rules before publishing, and a brand failure keeps the post as a draft.

steps.title: The calendar keeps it honest
steps.body: What is planned, what is drafted, what is approved and what is published, with the keyword each piece is for.

limits.free: 50 AI-written posts per company, for ever. Content clusters, the strategy calendar and Blog Studio are all included.
limits.paid: Growth adds 300 posts a month and Auto Blog; Business adds 1,500 a month.
limits.cannot: Auto Blog, the unattended daily publisher, is not on the free plan. And volume is not the pitch — the cap is 50 for a reason.

faqs.question: Is this another AI slop generator?
faqs.answer: A human approves every post, a brand check runs on each one, and the free cap is 50 for ever. If volume were the pitch, that cap would be a strange way to sell it.

faqs.question: Does the AI see my other customers’ content?
faqs.answer: No. One customer’s content never appears in another customer’s prompt.

platform.name: Competitive and market intel
platform.summary: Competitors, AI research, Market Radar and page opportunities.
platform.problem: Competitive research is usually a one-off: someone does a deep dive, writes a deck, and the deck is out of date within a month. Meanwhile the pages your competitors quietly published last week are the ones taking your traffic.

steps.title: Keep a competitor list that stays current
steps.body: The sites you actually compete with, tracked rather than researched once.

steps.title: Find the pages you have not written
steps.body: Page opportunities: queries where competitors rank and you have nothing, ranked by what they would be worth to you.

steps.title: Run research when you need depth
steps.body: AI-assisted research for a market or a segment, when a question needs more than a list.

limits.paid: AI research and the market intelligence workspace are on Growth and Business.
limits.cannot: We do not estimate a competitor’s traffic and present it as fact. Where a number is modelled rather than measured, the page says so.

faqs.question: Do you show competitor traffic estimates?
faqs.answer: We show what we can measure and label what is modelled. Precise-looking traffic estimates for somebody else’s site are guesses with error bars nobody prints.

platform.name: Site intelligence and ops
platform.summary: Field and lab speed, crawl health, demand, the page report card, Connect and team roles.
platform.problem: Speed tooling gives you a score out of 100 from a lab test on a machine nothing like your visitor’s phone. Meanwhile the actual question — is this page getting slower, and does it matter — goes unanswered.

steps.title: Connect your site once
steps.body: A five-step flow connects Search Console, analytics and the crawler. It is the first thing you do and it takes a couple of minutes.

steps.title: Field data alongside lab data
steps.body: Real-user measurements where they are available, next to the lab numbers, so you can tell a real regression from a noisy test.

steps.title: Read the page report card
steps.body: Per page: speed, demand, issues and content state, in one view, instead of four tools.

steps.title: Work the site checklist to green
steps.body: The same checklist we hold our own sites to. If ours is not green, we have no business selling it.

limits.free: Site Intelligence in full on one website, with Search Console, GA4 and Clarity connected, on a weekly cadence.
limits.cannot: Field data only exists where there is enough real traffic to report it. On a quiet site you will see lab numbers only, and the page says which is which.

faqs.question: Is this a PageSpeed Insights wrapper?
faqs.answer: No. We measure from our own crawl and read field data where it exists, then track it over time against the rest of your SEO state.

platform.name: Publishing
platform.summary: The release, approve, publish and rollback loop — and exactly where it can publish.
platform.problem: Every SEO tool stops at the recommendation. The gap between "your title should say X" and your title actually saying X is where SEO projects die — it needs a developer, a deploy and a reason to prioritise it.

steps.title: Changes are grouped into a release
steps.body: Not a stream of individual edits. A release is a reviewable set with a diff.

steps.title: Someone approves it
steps.body: The approval is recorded: who, what and when. This is not optional.

steps.title: It publishes where it can
steps.body: On a supported platform the release is applied directly to your site.

steps.title: Everywhere else, you get the exact change and an export
steps.body: The precise before and after, and a file you can apply. You are never guessing what to paste where.

steps.title: The rollback is one click
steps.body: The history keeps what changed and lets you reverse it.

limits.free: The full release, approve, publish and rollback loop on one website.
limits.paid: Same loop, more sites and a higher cadence.
limits.cannot: Direct publishing depends on your platform having a supported path. Where it does not, you get a staged change set, a diff and an export — which is honest, and still far more than a recommendation. The current capability list lives in the docs and we keep it current.

faqs.question: Which platforms can you publish to directly?
faqs.answer: The capability list is in the docs rather than on this page, because it changes. If yours is not on it, the export path still works and nothing else about the product changes.

faqs.question: What if a published change makes things worse?
faqs.answer: Roll it back from the history. The previous state is kept precisely so that is one click.

platform.name: Roles and permissions
platform.summary: Organizations, roles and per-site scoping, enforced in the database.
platform.problem: Most SEO tools model your clients as "projects" in one account. That means a junior who needs to read one report can see all of them, and your isolation is a UI filter rather than a boundary.

steps.title: A company is the unit, not a project
steps.body: Each client is an organization with its own sites, its own members and its own roles.

steps.title: Isolation is enforced in the database
steps.body: Row-level security on every table, not a check in the application layer that a bug can skip.

steps.title: Scope a member to specific sites
steps.body: Someone can be given one site rather than all of them, with the permissions they actually need.

steps.title: Permissions are per section
steps.body: Reading the blog list does not silently grant the ability to spend AI credits. Those are separate permissions on purpose.

limits.free: Two team members on one website, with the full role model.
limits.paid: Growth allows ten members; Business is unlimited.
limits.cannot: Single sign-on and SCIM provisioning are not built. If you need them, say so and we will tell you honestly where that sits.

faqs.question: How is tenant isolation actually enforced?
faqs.answer: By row-level security policies in the database, so a query from one company cannot return another company’s rows even if application code gets it wrong.

platform.name: API and MCP
platform.summary: The public API and the MCP server, on the Business plan.
platform.problem: If SEO data cannot reach your own dashboards, your own scripts and your own agents, it stays in somebody else’s interface and never becomes part of how you actually work.

steps.title: A REST API over your own data
steps.body: Sites, audits, findings, keywords and content, scoped to your organization.

steps.title: An MCP server for agents
steps.body: The same data exposed so an AI agent can read it directly, with your organization’s permissions applied.

steps.title: Scoped keys
steps.body: Keys carry the same per-site scoping as a member, so an integration gets exactly what it needs.

limits.cannot: It is a read and management API for your own organization. It is not a data product, and it does not resell keyword or backlink data.

faqs.question: Is there a free API tier?
faqs.answer: No. The API and the MCP server are on the Business plan.

solutions.name: SEO agencies
solutions.description: Run SEO for many clients with real isolation, per-site roles and per-site pricing. Each client is a company in the database, not a folder in your account.
solutions.problem: You are running SEO for eight clients on a spreadsheet and one expensive seat that three people share. The junior who needs to read one report can see all eight, your "client separation" is a dropdown filter, and you pay per seat for someone who only needs view access.

behaviours.title: Each client is an organization, not a project
behaviours.body: Its own sites, its own members, its own roles — and isolation enforced by row-level security in the database rather than a filter in the interface.

behaviours.title: Scope a member to one site
behaviours.body: A contractor working on one client gets exactly that client. A junior who needs to read reports gets read access to what they need and nothing else.

behaviours.title: Priced per site, not per seat
behaviours.body: Adding a reviewer does not add to the bill. That is the pricing model agencies ask for and rarely get.

behaviours.title: The fix ships, so the retainer shows work
behaviours.body: A release with an approval trail is a far better monthly report than a list of recommendations nobody actioned.

checklist: One organization per client, never a shared account
Scope every contractor to the sites they work on
Connect each client’s own Search Console through their own grant
Use releases so the approval trail is the client report
Keep a per-client site checklist and work it to green

faqs.question: Can my client see their own data without seeing other clients?
faqs.answer: Yes. Each client is a separate organization and isolation is enforced in the database, so a query from one cannot return another’s rows.

faqs.question: Do I pay for every person who logs in?
faqs.answer: No. Pricing is per website. Seats are included per plan rather than charged individually.

solutions.name: E-commerce
solutions.description: Catalogue SEO without the spreadsheet: duplicate variant pages, facet URLs eating crawl budget, thin categories and images that are too heavy.
solutions.problem: Your catalogue generates more URLs than anyone intended. Facets multiply, variants duplicate, categories with four products read as thin, and the hero images are two megabytes each. None of it is a bug, so nothing flags it.

behaviours.title: Crawl intelligence finds the URL explosion
behaviours.body: Click depth and crawl-budget consumption per section, so you can see which facet combination is generating ten thousand near-identical pages.

behaviours.title: URL triage groups the duplicates
behaviours.body: Variant pages competing for one query are grouped so you can canonicalise, merge or differentiate them deliberately.

behaviours.title: Image SEO across the catalogue
behaviours.body: Missing alt text, oversized files and the wrong format, counted across every product page rather than spot-checked.

behaviours.title: Product schema validated, not assumed
behaviours.body: Structured data checked for the properties rich results actually need, instead of trusting the theme that generated it.

checklist: Decide which facet URLs should be indexable, and block the rest
Canonicalise variants to a single product page
Give thin category pages genuine copy or merge them
Serve product images as AVIF or WebP at display size
Validate Product and Offer schema on a sample of real pages
Keep out-of-stock pages returning 200 with a clear state, not 404

faqs.question: Will it crawl my whole catalogue?
faqs.answer: On the free plan it crawls up to 500 URLs per run, which samples a catalogue rather than covering it. Growth raises that to 10,000 and Business to 100,000.

solutions.name: SaaS
solutions.description: SaaS SEO is feature pages, comparison pages and documentation. We audit all three, draft the fix, and publish it after approval.
solutions.problem: Your marketing site gets attention and your documentation does not, even though docs answer the long-tail questions buyers actually search. Meanwhile your feature pages all share one meta description because they came from the same template.

behaviours.title: Templated pages are caught as duplicates
behaviours.body: Pages sharing a title or description are grouped, which is exactly what a templated feature or integration set produces.

behaviours.title: The Question Bank finds buyer questions
behaviours.body: The full-sentence questions people ask about a category — the shape that matters now answers come from assistants as well as results pages.

behaviours.title: AI-answer visibility is measured
behaviours.body: Traffic arriving from AI assistants is reported separately, so you can see whether your docs are being used as a source.

behaviours.title: Content clusters give the docs a shape
behaviours.body: A hub and its supporting pages, so documentation feeds the cluster instead of sitting beside it.

checklist: Give every feature page a title and description that is true of it alone
Make sure docs are crawlable and in the sitemap
Build one comparison page per serious competitor, honestly
Group docs into clusters with a hub page
Track which pages AI assistants are citing

faqs.question: Can it audit a docs site on a subdomain?
faqs.answer: Yes. Subdomains added to the same site record count as one website, so docs.example.com and example.com are covered together on the free plan.

solutions.name: Local business
solutions.description: Location pages that actually carry local signals, consistent details, and the review platforms you are missing. One location free, for ever.
solutions.problem: You have a website, a Google listing and a nagging sense that competitors with worse work are above you. Usually it is the boring things: an address written three ways, a location page that never names the suburb, and four review platforms you have never heard of.

behaviours.title: A location registry, not a page
behaviours.body: Each location with its address, hours and service area recorded once, so the details stop drifting between pages.

behaviours.title: Landing-page checks per location
behaviours.body: Whether each location page carries the signals a local result needs, and which pages are duplicates with the city swapped.

behaviours.title: The review-platform checklist
behaviours.body: The platforms relevant to your sector, which you are on, and which you are not. The gap is usually the finding.

checklist: Write the business name, address and phone number identically everywhere
Give each location its own page with genuinely local content
Add LocalBusiness schema with the real opening hours
Claim the review platforms your sector uses
Make sure the phone number is a link on mobile

faqs.question: Is one location really enough on the free plan?
faqs.answer: For a single-site business, yes — that is the whole job. Growth covers 25 locations if you expand.

solutions.name: Publishers
solutions.description: Large archives have specific problems: content decay, crawl budget spent on pages nobody reads, and index bloat. We measure all three.
solutions.problem: You have twelve years of articles. A tenth of them bring almost all the traffic, a third have decayed quietly, and the crawler is spending its time on tag pages from 2014. Nobody has the hours to go through it by hand.

behaviours.title: Crawl intelligence shows where budget goes
behaviours.body: Click depth, orphan pages and the sections consuming crawl budget without earning it — the archive question, answered with numbers.

behaviours.title: Rankings tied to the page that holds them
behaviours.body: When a position drops, you see which URL lost it, which is how you find decay instead of guessing at it.

behaviours.title: Internal linking from your own archive
behaviours.body: Suggestions drawn from content you already have, which is where a large archive has an advantage nothing else can match.

behaviours.title: Image search inventory across the archive
behaviours.body: Years of images with no alt text are both an accessibility problem and unindexed inventory.

checklist: Find and fix orphan pages in the archive
Decide which tag and date archives should be indexable
Refresh or consolidate decayed articles rather than deleting them
Add internal links from old articles to current hubs
Keep the sitemap limited to pages worth crawling

faqs.question: Can it handle an archive of 100,000 pages?
faqs.answer: Business crawls up to 100,000 URLs per run. The free plan samples 500, which is enough to find the patterns but not to cover an archive that size.

solutions.name: Developers
solutions.description: SEO as reviewable changes: a redirect map you can edit, a 404 monitor that watches what actually breaks, and an API and MCP server.
solutions.problem: SEO reaches you as a spreadsheet from someone else, with no context about which rows matter and no way to tell whether last month’s changes helped. Then you are asked to action 400 of them before Friday.

behaviours.title: Changes are releases with diffs
behaviours.body: A reviewable set with a before and after, an approval and a rollback — the workflow you already use, applied to SEO.

behaviours.title: Sitemaps, robots and redirects as managed state
behaviours.body: A redirect map you can edit and version, robots rules you can test, and a 404 monitor that reports what is actually breaking.

behaviours.title: An API and an MCP server
behaviours.body: Read your own audits, findings and keywords from your own scripts, dashboards or agents.

behaviours.title: Findings ranked by cost, not count
behaviours.body: A noindex in production outranks a short title. The list is ordered so the first thing you fix is the thing worth fixing.

checklist: Serve a correct sitemap and declare it in robots.txt
Collapse redirect chains to a single hop
Return the right status codes, including 410 for genuinely gone pages
Set canonical, lang and viewport on every template
Keep render-blocking resources out of the head
Watch for a noindex escaping from staging

faqs.question: Is the API available on the free plan?
faqs.answer: No. The API and the MCP server are on the Business plan.

faqs.question: Does the free audit render JavaScript?
faqs.answer: No. The public tools fetch and parse without rendering, which is one less abuse vector and one less bill. A page built entirely client-side will look emptier to the public tool than it does to you.

faq.question: Is it really free?
faq.answer: Yes, for one website, with the limits published on this page. No card, no expiry, and not limited to a single person — you get two seats.

faq.question: What is the catch?
faq.answer: More websites, more AI, a bigger team, PR and Media, and the API are paid. That is the whole catch, and it is on the pricing page rather than hidden in your head.

faq.question: Will you change the free plan later?
faq.answer: If we ever reduce it, companies already on the free plan keep the limits they signed up with. The limits are versioned and dated on this site, with a changelog.

faq.question: Do I need a credit card?
faq.answer: No. There is no card field in signup, because there is nothing to charge you for on the free plan.

faq.question: How many AI blog posts do I get?
faq.answer: Fifty per company, for ever. Only a post that is actually written counts, and a meter shows your remaining balance before you spend it — the same number the product enforces.

faq.question: Can it publish changes to my site?
faq.answer: On supported platforms, yes — it publishes after a human approves, and keeps a rollback. Everywhere else it prepares the exact change, shows you the diff and hands you an export. The capability list is in the docs.

faq.question: Do you crawl my site politely?
faq.answer: Yes. We send an identified user-agent, respect robots.txt, cap how many pages we fetch in one run, and publish those limits. We sell SEO; crawling badly would be a strange way to do it.

faq.question: What do you store when I use a free tool without an account?
faq.answer: The tool you ran, your site hostname, a hashed IP and timings. Not the query string, not the page content, and nothing that identifies you personally.

faq.question: How is this different from Google Search Console?
faq.answer: Search Console tells you what happened. We tell you what to change, draft the change, publish it once a human approves, and keep a rollback. We also read five engines Search Console does not.

faq.question: Can I use it for client sites?
faq.answer: Yes. Each client is a company with its own sites, members and roles, isolated in the database. You pay per site, not per seat.

faq.question: Is my data used to train AI?
faq.answer: No. Your content is never used in another customer’s prompt, never sold, and never used to train a public model.

faq.question: Can I export everything and leave?
faq.answer: Yes. Export is self-serve, and the deletion path is documented and tested rather than promised.

faq.question: Who is behind it?
faq.answer: Meru Technosoft — the team behind HelloGrowthCRM, HelloBooks and HelloTime. This is the SEO platform we built to run our own sites, opened up.

checklist.label: Can it be found at all
checklist.intro: Start here. Everything below is wasted if the answer to any of these is no.

items.title: The site is served over HTTPS
items.why: Browsers mark http as not secure, and https has been a ranking signal for years.

items.title: No noindex left in production
items.why: A noindex that escaped from staging removes the page from search entirely. It is the most expensive accident in SEO.

items.title: robots.txt does not block what you want indexed
items.why: One stray Disallow line can remove a whole section from every search engine.

items.title: An XML sitemap exists and is declared in robots.txt
items.why: It is how a new or deep page gets discovered in days rather than weeks.

items.title: The sitemap only lists live, canonical, indexable URLs
items.why: A sitemap full of redirects and 404s teaches crawlers to trust it less.

items.title: Search Console and Bing Webmaster Tools are verified
items.why: They are the only direct report of what the engines actually see.

checklist.label: On-page basics
checklist.intro: The highest-leverage things on a page, and the most likely to have been written once and forgotten.

items.title: Every page has a unique title of roughly 50–60 characters
items.why: The title is the strongest on-page signal and the clickable line in every result.

items.title: Every page has a unique meta description
items.why: Without one the engine writes its own snippet, and it is rarely the pitch you would choose.

items.title: Exactly one H1 per page, and headings in order
items.why: The outline is what screen readers and crawlers use to understand the page.

items.title: A self-referencing canonical on every page
items.why: Without it, parameter and duplicate URLs can be indexed instead of the one you want.

items.title: No thin pages competing for the same query
items.why: Two pages for one intent means neither wins cleanly. Merge or differentiate them.

items.title: Open Graph and Twitter card tags are present
items.why: Without them a shared link renders as a bare URL instead of a preview.

checklist.label: Technical health
checklist.intro: The things that fail quietly, with no error, until traffic has already gone.

items.title: No broken internal links
items.why: They waste crawl budget, lose link equity, and send real visitors to a dead end.

items.title: Redirect chains collapsed to a single hop
items.why: Every hop costs time and loses a little signal.

items.title: Permanent moves use 301, not 302
items.why: A temporary redirect tells engines to keep the old URL indexed.

items.title: Gone pages return 404 or 410, not a soft 200
items.why: A "not found" page returning 200 gets indexed as a real page.

items.title: No mixed content on HTTPS pages
items.why: Browsers block or warn on it, which breaks the page and the padlock.

items.title: Structured data parses and has its required properties
items.why: Invalid JSON-LD is ignored entirely, so the markup does nothing at all.

checklist.label: Speed and mobile
checklist.intro: Measured, not guessed. Most of this is images.

items.title: Time to first byte under about 800ms
items.why: Everything else waits for the first byte, so a slow server delays every Core Web Vital.

items.title: Text responses are compressed
items.why: Compression typically cuts HTML transfer by about 70% for one line of server config.

items.title: Images served as AVIF or WebP at display size
items.why: Oversized images are usually the single biggest cause of a slow page on mobile.

items.title: Images have width and height set
items.why: Without them the page jumps as images load, which is cumulative layout shift.

items.title: Every meaningful image has alt text
items.why: Screen readers cannot describe them and image search cannot index them.

items.title: A viewport meta tag is present
items.why: Without it mobile browsers render at desktop width and zoom out.

checklist.label: Content and intent
checklist.intro: The part no tool can check for you, which is why it is the part that decides the outcome.

items.title: Each page answers one query, in the first sixty words
items.why: If the answer is below the fold, the visitor is already back on the results page.

items.title: Each page says something the top results do not
items.why: Matching the existing answers is how you rank eleventh.

items.title: Related pages link to each other with descriptive anchors
items.why: Internal linking is the cheapest ranking improvement available and almost nobody does it.

items.title: Every page is within three clicks of the home page
items.why: Click depth is a strong predictor of how often a page is re-crawled.

items.title: Updated pages have an honest dateModified
items.why: Bumping the date without changing the content is a trick engines learned to ignore.

items.title: Content has a real, attributable author
items.why: An "Admin" byline tells a reader nothing and helps nothing.

checklist.label: Beyond Google
checklist.intro: Usually skipped entirely, which is exactly why it is worth doing.

items.title: Bing Webmaster Tools is verified
items.why: Bing powers more search than most people assume, including several AI assistants.

items.title: IndexNow is set up for new and changed URLs
items.why: It pushes URLs to Bing, Yandex and Seznam instead of waiting to be discovered.

items.title: If you serve several languages, hreflang return tags are correct
items.why: Without a return tag the whole hreflang set is ignored, which is where most setups break.

items.title: You have decided, deliberately, whether AI crawlers may read your content
items.why: Either answer is defensible. Not having decided is the problem.

items.title: An llms.txt exists if you want to be summarised accurately
items.why: Cheap, and it gives an assistant a correct description rather than a guessed one.
